title: Dying at Maghar
hookLine: believing the holy city promised no special freedom, Kabir went to die at Maghar, a place thought unlucky (Kabir, Gauri)

lines: KASHI — THE CITY OF THE PROMISE.
cards: Some places carry a promise. Pilgrims in Kabir's world believed that whoever died in Kashi, the holy city of Benares, would be set free.
Another town, Maghar, had the opposite reputation: die there, people said, and your next birth would be a poor one. Kabir lived his whole life in Kashi.
Then, near the end, by his own account in a hymn, he got up and went to Maghar.

teach.h: MY WHOLE LIFE IN SHIVA'S CITY.
teach.b: The hymn is in Raag Gauri, on Ang 326. Its turn, in paraphrase: my whole life I spent in Shiva's city, and at the time of death I rose and came to Maghar. Then the sharp question.

teach.h: WHAT FAVOR WOULD I OWE THE LORD?
teach.b: If Kabir leaves his body in Kashi, what favor would he owe the Lord? If the city does the saving, the Lord has nothing left to do.
A promise tied to a place sounds generous, but it quietly moves freedom out of the heart and onto a map. Kabir refuses the trade. He'd rather owe everything to the Lord than owe it to an address.
In another hymn he puts it flatly, in paraphrase: to one who has the Lord in the heart, Kashi and Maghar are the same. So the walk to Maghar isn't a stunt. It's the hymn acted out.
And Kabir doesn't mock the pilgrims or call the holy city bad. He says it isn't the thing that saves. A place can be dear, can help you remember, can be full of people praying.
Sikhs travel to historic gurdwaras, too. The Gurus taught that the bath that counts is in the Name, not only the water.

teach.h: THE LUCKY SHIRT, THE SAME QUESTION.
teach.b: Some superstitions today are smaller: the lucky shirt, the seat always taken, the step never skipped.
They look harmless. Kabir's question still fits them. If the shirt does the work, what's left for you, and what's left for God?

how: Sikhs read Kabir's Maghar hymn as part of Gurbani, and Sikh teaching holds that liberation comes through the Name and grace, not through dying in a particular holy place.

o: the holy city where dying was said to set a person free
the town thought unlucky to die in, where Kabir went at the end
the river where Kabir's family washed the cloth they wove

games.q: inside the hymn — tap the pairs.

s: Kabir mocks the pilgrims who go to Kashi
he doesn't call the city bad; he says it isn't what saves.
Kabir says that to one with the Lord in the heart, Kashi and Maghar are the same
he says it in another hymn, and acts it out by going to Maghar.
in the Gauri hymn, Kabir goes to Maghar near the end of his life
my whole life I spent in Shiva's city, and at the time of death I came to Maghar.

games.q: you've lived your whole life in the holy city that promises freedom to those who die there. the end is near. what do you do?
o: leave for the town thought unlucky.
go on pilgrimage to a third place.
games.why: Kabir went to Maghar. if Kashi did the saving, he asks, what favor would he owe the Lord?

practice: Let your mind look for one small habit kept for luck, if you have one: a seat, the order of your morning, a number you avoid; if none comes, take any fixed habit.
Just notice it, without scolding, and picture doing it the other way once, feeling what's left when the charm is gone. If you pray, you can say Waheguru on each breath out.

wordCard.voice: Maghar. The town thought unlucky to die in, where Kabir went at the end, because the place doesn't do the saving.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: the town Kabir went to at the end, thought unlucky to die in.

carryVoice: Your line: the place doesn't save you. With the Lord in the heart, Kashi and Maghar are the same. See you tomorrow.

sources.ref: Ramkali, Kabir, Ang 969 (kia kasi kia ukhar magahar)
